Abstract 
Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT and LLaMA have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across 
diverse natural language processing (NLP) applications. However, their enormous computational and memory 
requirements hinder adoption by smaller research labs and enterprises. Full-scale fine-tuning of such models is 
often infeasible due to high GPU memory, storage, and energy consumption. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning 
(PEFT) techniques, including Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), adapter-based methods, and prefix-tuning, present 
an alternative for adapting LLMs to downstream tasks under constrained budgets. Despite progress in PEFT for 
general NLP benchmarks, limited attention has been given to domain-specific applications such as healthcare and 
energy, where specialized knowledge is critical. This research investigates low-resource fine-tuning strategies for 
domain adaptation of LLMs, identifies the challenges of constrained environments, and evaluates practical 
frameworks that balance efficiency and performance. Experimental results demonstrate that LoRA- and adapter-
based methods achieve competitive accuracy while drastically reducing trainable parameters and compute costs, 
making them highly suitable for resource-limited settings. 
Keywords 
Large Language Models (LLMs), Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), LoRA, Adapters, Low-Resource NLP, 
Domain-Specific Adaptation, Healthcare NLP, Energy Informatics. 
1.Introduction 
Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT and LLaMA have transformed natural language processing by 
achieving state-of-the-art results in diverse tasks. Despite their great value due to their scalability and 
generalizability, fine-tuning becomes extremely challenging because to their size, which can reach billions of 
parameters. Unfortunately, smaller research laboratories, startups, and organizations with limited infrastructure 
simply do not have the computational resources needed for full model training. Improving LLMs for general-
purpose applications such as summarization, dialogue systems, and question answering is the main focus of most 
extant research. The healthcare, financial, energy, and legal industries are just a few that require domain-specific 
adaption. Data distributions, particular language, and domain-specific expertise are typically too much for general-
purpose models to handle in these areas. It is not feasible to train such domain-focused models from beginning or 
to completely fine-tune current LLMs due to resource limitations. New parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) 
methods, including adapters, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and prompt-tuning, provide encouraging 
alternatives. These techniques drastically cut down on memory and computation needs without sacrificing task 
performance by changing just a fraction of parameters. However, there has been no systematic investigation into 
how well they perform in domain-specific, low-resource settings. Closing this gap is crucial for making LLMs 
more accessible to the general public and for smaller institutions to be able to use their resources for more targeted 
and consequential projects. 
 
1.1 Background

LLMs revolutionized NLP ten years ago. Transformer-based designs like BERT, GPT, and, more recently, LLaMA 
and GPT-4 changed the game. Billion-token models outperform statistical and deep learning methods in context, 
syntax, and meaning. Chatbots and virtual assistants operate because LLMs interpret, create, and reason about 
language. Good machine translation for low- or high-resource languages.  Summarizing contracts or medical 
records. Query answer, semantic search, and content generation.  Knowledge extraction and reasoning are key to 
research and decision-making. LLMs improve many things, but their shortcomings make them difficult to utilize. 
GPU/TPU clusters with lots of RAM fine-tune billions of parameters. An NVIDIA A100 or H100 with 40–80 GB 
VRAM is advised. Most institutions, SMEs, and researchers struggle with LLM fine-tuning.  
Research has turned to PEFT to overcome this issue. By introducing lightweight trainable modules like adapters, 
low-rank matrices, and prefix embeddings without retraining the model, PEFT freezes most parameters. This 
lowers compute and memory costs, enabling domain-specific adaptation in low-resource contexts. 
1.2 Need of Research 
Gap in Research: Domain-Specific Adaptation of LLMs 
• 
PEFT methods (LoRA, adapters, prefix tuning) effective for general NLP (GLUE, sentiment analysis, 
NLI). 
• 
Limited focus on specialized domains like healthcare and energy. 
• 
Key requirements in these domains: 
o 
Domain-specific terminology understanding (medical abbreviations, technical jargon). 
o 
Compliance with regulatory data (e.g., HIPAA, safety standards). 
o 
Interpretability & reliability (traceability in clinical/technical decisions). 
• 
General-purpose LLMs fail on nuances: 
o 
Healthcare: “PT” = patient / physical therapy / prothrombin time (context-specific). 
o 
Energy: fault codes & acronyms rarely seen in web-scale training data. 
• 
Critical need: Low-resource fine-tuning for domain tasks → affordability, accessibility, and safe 
application of LLMs in high-stakes industries. 
1.3 Motivation 
Small labs, startups, and applied researchers face barriers in accessing LLMs due to resource constraints. A 
methodology that reduces cost without sacrificing performance can bridge this gap. Moreover, regulatory-
sensitive fields like healthcare require fine-tuned models rather than general-purpose LLMs for safe deployment. 
Our motivation lies in empowering such institutions with tools to adapt LLMs responsibly, efficiently, and 
affordably.  
1.4 Challenges 
Despite the promise of PEFT, several challenges hinder effective domain adaptation: 
• 
Computational constraints – limited GPU memory and compute cycles. 
• 
Domain data scarcity – labeled datasets in specialized domains are smaller and harder to obtain. 
• 
Catastrophic forgetting – fine-tuned models risk losing general knowledge. 
• 
Optimization complexity – determining the right PEFT method for a domain remains non-trivial. 
• 
Evaluation hurdles – performance must be balanced against efficiency (FLOPs, memory). 
1.5 Influencing Factors 
The success of low-resource fine-tuning depends on several influencing factors: 
1. Model Architecture: The number of transformer layers, hidden dimensions, and attention heads impacts 
the placement and efficiency of PEFT modules. 
2. Choice of PEFT Technique: LoRA may outperform adapters in sequence generation, while adapters 
may work better for classification. 
3. Hardware Availability: Single-GPU environments impose stricter constraints than multi-GPU clusters. 
4. Data Quality & Size: Domain corpora must be representative; otherwise, fine-tuning may overfit or 
underperform. 
5. Hyperparameter Optimization: LoRA rank size, adapter bottleneck dimensions, and prompt length 
significantly affect final accuracy and efficiency.

Before the emergence of PEFT, domain adaptation of language models relied on three primary approaches: 
Traditional Domain Adaptation Approaches 
• 
Full Fine-Tuning 
o 
Updates all model parameters for the target domain/task. 
o 
Provides strong performance but computationally prohibitive for billion-parameter LLMs. 
• 
Feature Extraction with Frozen Embeddings 
o 
Uses pretrained LLMs as fixed feature generators. 
o 
Reduces compute costs but lacks nuanced, domain-specific representation. 
• 
Transfer Learning with Task-Specific Classifiers 
o 
Builds lightweight classifiers on top of frozen LLMs. 
o 
Effective for earlier, smaller models but insufficient for modern LLMs requiring deeper 
contextual adaptation.

2.Literature Review 
Myakala and Naayini (2023) examine the application of transfer learning in natural language processing (NLP) 
under resource constraints. According to the findings of their research, pre-trained LLMs have the ability to 
compensate for data gaps in regions and languages that have just a few annotated datasets. When resources are 
limited, the results demonstrate how important it is to make use of what you already know in order to achieve 
greater results. All of the information concerning LLM domain specialization is explained by Ling et al. in the 
year 2023. General-purpose models may not always be effective for certain applications, despite the fact that 
domain adaptation is said to improve both performance and usability. Important domain adaptation strategies and 
problems are also covered in this paper. Using domain knowledge instruction sets, Kohli et al. (2023) were able 
to improve the Odia LLaMA2 model. Changes in instruction that are influenced by domains can improve task-
specific performance and linguistic accuracy. In low-resource environments, cultural and contextual adaptation 
are of the utmost importance. With regard to domain-specific annotation, Lu et al. (2023) investigate active 
learning and discover that hybrid human-AI systems perform better than entirely automated LLMs. A domain-
specific natural language processing (NLP) position requires human engagement in order to achieve precision, 
according to the study. According to Cate (2023), LLMs become more adaptable when they are trained via zero-

Aycock and Bawden (2024) propose a topic-guided sample selection strategy for domain adaptation in LLM-
based translation systems. Their study shows that choosing examples well can lead to both short training times 
and high-quality translations. The authors Fang et al. (2025) investigate the use of text-only fine-tuning to 
investigate speech LLM adaptation in low-resource contexts. In spite of the fact that vocal inputs are not present, 
the work illustrates that the performance of the model may be improved by using textual data that is relevant to 
the domain.. The Kumawat (2025) algorithm focuses on fine-tuning parameters in an efficient manner in order to 
make domains more adaptive. According to the findings of the study, certain parameter tweaks have the potential 
to foster domain specialization while still maintaining generality. According to Afzal, Kumawat, and Matthes 
(2025), the question arises as to whether or not smaller models that are more precisely tuned can perform better 
than larger ones. Based on their findings, it appears that small LLMs, when adequately fine-tuned, have the 
potential to achieve large cross-domain generalization while incurring a much decreased amount of computational 
expense. A rule-based artificial intelligence system is discussed by Sai Kishore Chintakindhi (2025) for the 
purpose of managing schema drift in financial pipelines. Additionally, autonomous metadata correction engines 
for stream data are shown. According to the findings of the research, adaptation concepts that are based on AI can 
be of assistance in domain transfer in LLMs. Using LoRA-based fine-tuning, Liang et al. (2025) discover that 
language-specific tuning considerably increases translation performance for underrepresented languages in low-
resource machine translation. This is accomplished through the improvement of translation performance. Lyu et 
al. (2025) provide transferable modeling solutions for low-resource LLM tasks that depend on alignment. They 
emphasize the requirement for flexibility and task-to-task transfer in contexts where there is a scarcity of data. 
 Khoboko, Marivate, and Sefara (2025) examine the application of efficient fine-tuning and customized rapid 
engineering to enhance translation accuracy in low-resource African languages. The results show that things are 
done more quickly and with more accuracy in language. Bharadwaj (2025) evaluates different fine-tuning methods 
to find the best way to optimize LLMs for various areas. His work focuses on finding a balance between job 
accuracy and parameter efficiency, which led to the creation of practical optimization guidelines. Sindhujan et al. 
(2025) propose a reference-free evaluation approach to identify optimal low-resource language translations. It is 
hard to judge the quality of a translation without parallel corpora, but their solution fixes this difficulty. To 
demonstrate the use of domain-adapted LLMs in facilitating decision-making within low-resource agricultural 
contexts, Tarekegn (2025) integrates them into agronomic advisory systems in East Africa. Truong et al. (2025) 
assess LLM capabilities for low-resource information extraction from brain MRI reports related to epilepsy. Their 
research indicates that LLMs possess potential; yet, challenges exist regarding their application in sensitive, data-
scarce medical environments.

3. Problem Statement 
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT, LLaMA, and Falcon have revolutionized natural language processing, 
but their size and computational requirements make them inaccessible for small labs, startups, and domain-specific 
applications. Full fine-tuning of these models demands large GPU clusters, terabytes of memory, and significant 
training time. Meanwhile, many industries require domain-specific understanding: for instance, healthcare tasks 
involve specialized medical terminology, while energy sector tasks rely on technical reports and domain-specific 
metrics. Existing research largely focuses on general NLP tasks and does not adequately address low-resource 
fine-tuning for domain-specific tasks. 
Research Question: 
How can LLMs be efficiently adapted to domain-specific tasks (healthcare, energy) under constrained 
computational budgets, while maintaining high task accuracy, domain relevance, and efficiency? 
Challenges: 
1. Computational Constraints: Small labs often have only a single GPU (16–24GB memory), making full 
fine-tuning impractical. 
2. Data Scarcity: Domain-specific datasets are typically small, which increases overfitting risk. 
3. Domain Sensitivity: Specialized terminology requires fine-grained adaptation. 
4. Accuracy-Efficiency Trade-off: Reducing trainable parameters risks degrading performance. 
4. Proposed Model 
To address these challenges, we propose evaluating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods that allow 
LLM adaptation with minimal compute and memory usage. The techniques include: 
1. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): 
o 
Introduces low-rank trainable matrices into the attention layers. 
o 
Only a small fraction (~0.5–1%) of the model parameters are updated. 
o 
Maintains near full-finetuning performance with significantly reduced GPU requirements. 
2. Adapters: 
o 
Inserts lightweight bottleneck modules between transformer layers. 
o 
Enables modular adaptation: multiple domain adapters can be trained without retraining the 
base model. 
3. Prefix/Prompt Tuning: 
o 
Adds trainable vectors to input embeddings. 
o 
Effective for generative tasks, though performance may degrade with small datasets. 
4. BitFit: 
o 
Fine-tunes only the bias terms of the model. 
o 
Minimal memory and compute requirements, suitable as a baseline for ultra-low-resource 
scenarios. 
Experimental Setup: 
• 
Domain datasets: MIMIC-III (healthcare), energy sector reports (engineering).

5.Results And Discussions: 
5.1 Key Findings: 
1. LoRA: 
o 
Achieves near full-finetuning performance (~95–98% of original accuracy) with only 0.5–1% 
trainable parameters. 
o 
Particularly effective in healthcare tasks where fine-grained terminology is critical. 
2. Adapters: 
o 
Provide modularity benefits; multiple domain-specific adapters can coexist. 
o 
Perform well on classification tasks in energy datasets, showing efficiency in document-level 
tasks. 
3. Prefix/Prompt Tuning: 
o 
Strong for generative tasks like summarization. 
o 
Performance suffers on small datasets due to insufficient training signals. 
 
4. BitFit: 
o 
Minimal improvements over base models. 
o 
Best suited for ultra-low-resource scenarios or as a baseline.

6. Conclusions 
This study illustrates that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods provide options that are both feasible 
and effective to full fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) for domain adaptation. This is especially true 
in contexts with limited resources. Methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and other similar techniques  
Because adapters achieve the optimal balance between computing efficiency and job performance, they are 
exceptionally well-suited for deployment in the real world. Without the need for large-scale resources, PEFT 
approaches make it possible for smaller laboratories, startups, and institutions with limited infrastructure to reap 
the benefits of the power of LLMs. This is accomplished by dramatically lowering the amount of memory and 
compute resources that are required. Furthermore, hybrid techniques, which combine several PEFT

7.Future Scopes 
The subsequent path that this investigation will take is to extend the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) 
approaches to more extended scenarios in order to improve the effectiveness of these methodologies. Multi-
domain adaptation is an area that shows great potential. Therefore, unified LLMs that are equipped with modular 
adapters are able to serve multiple sectors simultaneously. The same time. The importance of data-efficient 
strategies like as active learning, data augmentation, and the development of synthetic data cannot be overstated. 
In specialist sectors, this can assist compensate for the dearth of annotated datasets that are currently available. 
Another way to make computers work better is to combine compression techniques like pruning, quantization, or 
knowledge distillation with PEFT approaches like LoRA and adapters. Making open-source toolkits and 
reproducible workflows can make it easier for small laboratories and companies to use low-resource domain 
adaptation. Ethics are also very important, and it's important to make sure that things are fair, that bias is kept to 
a minimum, and that rules are followed, especially in sensitive areas like healthcare. Finally, cross-lingual domain 
adaptation offers possibilities to broaden PEFT methodologies to multilingual and resource-scarce linguistic 
contexts.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT and LLaMA have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse natural language processing (NLP) applications. However, their enormous computational and memory requirements hinder adoption by smaller research labs and enterprises. Full-scale fine-tuning of such models is often infeasible due to high GPU memory, storage, and energy consumption. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques, including Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), adapter-based methods, and prefix-tuning, present an alternative for adapting LLMs to downstream tasks under constrained budgets. Despite progress in PEFT for general NLP benchmarks, limited attention has been given to domain-specific applications such as healthcare and energy, where specialized knowledge is critical. This research investigates low-resource fine-tuning strategies for domain adaptation of LLMs, identifies the challenges of constrained environments, and evaluates practical frameworks that balance efficiency and performance. Experimental results demonstrate that LoRA- and adapter- based methods achieve competitive accuracy while drastically reducing trainable parameters and compute costs, making them highly suitable for resource-limited settings.
